Understanding Human Actions through
the Lens of Executable Models

Rimvydas Rubavicius(✉)    Manisha Dubey    N. Siddharth    Subramanian Ramamoorthy Affiliation: School of Informatics
The University of Edinburgh E-mail rimvydas.rubavicius@ed.ac.uk
Abstract

Human-centred systems require an understanding of human actions in the physical world. Temporally extended sequences of actions are intentional and structured, yet existing methods for recognising what actions are performed often do not attempt to capture their structure, particularly how the actions are executed. This, however, is crucial for assessing the quality of the action’s execution and its differences from other actions. To capture the internal mechanics of actions, we introduce a domain-specific language ExAct that represents human motions as underspecified motion programs, interpreted as reward-generating functions for zero-shot policy inference using forward-backwards representations. By leveraging the compositional nature of ExAct motion programs, we combine individual policies into an executable neuro-symbolic model that uses program structure for compositional modelling. We evaluate the utility of the proposed pipeline for creating executable action models by analysing motion-capture data to understand human actions, for the tasks of human action segmentation and action anomaly detection. Our results show that the use of executable action models improves data efficiency and captures intuitive relationships between actions compared with monolithic, task-specific approaches.

Keywords: 
Neuro-symbolic Approaches Executable Models Motion Programs Action Segmentation Action Anomaly Detection

1 Introduction

Consider a cook preparing hollandaise stirring exhibits a circular motion that not only represents whisking but also reflects their understanding of emulsification and their fixation and adaptation to the pot’s dimensions and heat intensity. A pause or a change in rhythm may signal a new action, such as adjusting the flame or picking ingredients. While the action is categorised as “stir”, this label, on its own, does not convey the action’s complexity: it does not account for the mechanics of the motion, its intentionality, or the relationships among their goals, the other actions they have taken and will take, and the environment.

Human motions in the physical world are intentional and structured: they are carried out in the environment to achieve a goal following a sequence of actions [1]. Contemporary approaches to understanding human action can recognise actions and anticipate changes in them from observations: they recognise what actions humans are performing as action labels [47], which in turn have been used to estimate plans and goals [34]. Nevertheless, such representation is limited, as it does not assess how humans perform the action. Such knowledge is necessary to assess the quality of the action and compare it to other actions in the environment. To reason about intentional human movement in the physical world, we advocate for an executable model that captures the action’s internal mechanics and structure. Executability in the form of a mental simulation is a key feature of the type of models humans construct when reasoning about actions [6, 22] by abstracting them to concepts and reasoning about their composition, leading to a rich set of compositional generative models [10] instead of a large monolithic model. Executable models of actions bring us closer to human-centred AI for assistance [49], as they enable assistive agents to reason about users’ errors when executing actions and, in turn, provide proactive assistance.

To this end, we study the utility of learning executable action models from observations in the form of human motion-capture (MoCap) data (see Fig. 1 for an overview). We introduce ExAct domain-specific language (DSL) that encodes intentional human movement as motion programs (§ 3.2). These programs use keypoints as a primitive for describing intentional human movement, but do so in an underspecified manner: they do not explicitly prescribe behaviour to every keypoint. This unique feature allows motion programs to be interpreted as reward-generating functions [7] that can be used for zero-shot policy inference [2, 43]. Using an ExAct grammar, we generate synthetic program-motion pairs and train a parser that, given human MoCap data, produces an motion program. Using motion programs, we describe a procedure for model building (§ 3.4) that aggregates individual motion programs by action label into an executable action model. By doing so, we leverage the robustness of neural networks and the compositionality of motion programs in creating a neuro-symbolic model, thereby going beyond labels to understand human actions.

We use our modelling approach to create executable action models from two benchmarks: the HumanAct12 [16] dataset and two datasets from EPFL-Smart-Kitchen (ESK) [3] of ESK Activities and ESK Verbs. We experiment with executable action models for two human action understanding tasks [46]: human action segmentation (§ 4.2), in which each timestep is assigned an activity label, and human action anomaly detection (§ 4.3), in which we assess how much a new instance of the action differs from previously observed action instances. Our experimental results establish that executable action models achieve greater data efficiency and compositional generalisation than task-specific models for human action understanding. Our contributions are summarised as follows:

  • •

    We design an ExAct DSL in which motion programs are interpreted as a reward-generating function for human-like motion generation.

  • •

    We formulate a model building procedure for executable action models using ExAct motion programs by, aggregating them into a compositional control policy with both neural and symbolic components.

  • •

    We learn a parser using an encoder-decoder architecture from MoCap data to ExAct motion programs using synthetic data.

  • •

    We demonstrate the benefits of executable action models relative to the baseline models for downstream human action understanding tasks, including human action segmentation, which yields effective data augmentation for MoCap data, and human action anomaly detection, which yields better insights into relationships among actions.

2 Related Work

2.1 Human Action Understanding

Various tasks are used to understand human actions from observations obtained with wearable, ambient, or vision sensors [40], with video data dominating the research landscape. Temporally extended observational data stream is processed to perform downstream tasks of localisation [50], recognition [18], segmentation [9], and anomaly detection [13] with each timestep analysed by categorising it with an action label [38, 35] or zero-shot captioning using vision-language models [29, 37]. In these downstream tasks, each action is represented as a language description (e g. a label or caption) rather than a model of an action itself. In our work, we restrict our attention to human MoCap data and use it to construct an executable action model based on ExAct motion programs, in which intentional human movements serve as primitives for building a compositional action model. Such an approach goes beyond language descriptions of actions to capture action’s internal mechanisms and intentionality.

2.2 Motion Programs

Programs have emerged as go-to representations for human cognition [42] supporting data-efficient adaptation as ad-hoc program synthesis when faced with novel scenarios [48] and growing the language of possible programs over time [11, 4]. Motion programs [24, 25] have been used for human action recognition and generation by using a three-level hierarchy of human poses, motion concepts (circular, linear, and stationary), and activity programs (procedural routines, including loops) with learning performed in estimating motion concepts from human poses and program synthesis from motion concepts. Our approach differs from such motion programs in that it is concept-free (i.e., without explicit motion concepts) and directly constructs motion programs from keypoints in the MoCap data. We achieve this by building a domain-specific language in which language predicates are based on keypoints of human poses that constitute intentional changes in movement, while abstracting away nuisance changes in other keypoints by utilising the underspecification in the human-like motion generation processes. This allows us to consider a wider range of motions, not constrained by motion concepts learned or engineered in the particular domain, at the cost of some generalisation capabilities from concept learning. In particular, even though ExAct motion programs and parser are based on the SPML kinematic model [31], it can, in principle, be changed to other kinematic models without a loss of generality of the proposed modelling approach.

2.3 Executable Models

Executable models [12, 5] are detailed models that capture the internal structure of the studied natural system (e g. human cell). Such models are designed to closely resemble the natural system and to serve as its surrogate for experiments and hypothesis testing. They can be seen as a kind of digital twin [39] that is process-centric: they mimic the underlying computational model of the natural system rather than focusing on perceptual realism and visual fidelity. Executable models can be seen as a kind of generative modelling in which, throughout the process of the computational model execution, the desired data is generated, linking them, in the context of this article, to human-like motion generation with [15, 52, 14] or without [36, 33, 32] conditioning of language prompt. In these generative models, however, model performance is measured based on the generated output rather than on the overall correctness and feasibility of the model, which are key desiderata of an executable model. Consequently, the executable action models we study complement such generative models: they allow not only the generation of motions but also the detection of anomalies in their assessment against the intended actions, thereby providing a more holistic understanding of human behaviour. By integrating symbolic reasoning with ExAct motion program with neural motion generation, we enable both qualitative and quantitative analysis of human actions, bridging the gap between recognition and reasoning.

3 Executable Action model

We describe components of constructing executable action models from MoCap data, including preliminaries (§ 3.1) on forward-backwards representations, ExAct DSL (§ 3.2), architecture and training procedure for the motion-to-program parser (§ 3.3), and the formulation of the model building (§ 3.4) procedure.

3.1 Preliminaries

We consider a humanoid agent in an embodied environment, represented by the SPML [31] kinematic model with 23 interconnected joints. The environment’s state representation 𝒔∈ℝ358{\bm{s}}\in\mathbb{R}^{358} 11 1 we focus on the state representation from Tirinzoni et al. [43], but in principle we can consider different state space from different humanoid agent environments. contains agent’s proprioceptive information, which includes joint position 𝒔pos∈ℝ69{\bm{s}}^{\mathrm{pos}}\in\mathbb{R}^{69} that is equivalent to the agent’s MoCap data and velocities 𝒔vel∈ℝ69{\bm{s}}^{\mathrm{vel}}\in\mathbb{R}^{69} in different 3D directions with respect to the agent’s coordinate frame while agent’s control signals (actions) 𝒂∈[−1,1]69{\bm{a}}\in[-1,1]^{69} describe the forces to be applied for each joint and their directions at every timestep. Motion 𝒔0:T=𝒔0,𝒔1,𝒔2…,𝒔T{\bm{s}}_{0:T}={\bm{s}}_{0},{\bm{s}}_{1},{\bm{s}}_{2}\dots,{\bm{s}}_{T} is a sequence of states in the environment as generated by a sequence of actions 𝒂1:T−1=𝒂1,𝒂2,…,𝒂T−1{\bm{a}}_{1:T-1}={\bm{a}}_{1},{\bm{a}}_{2},\dots,{\bm{a}}_{T-1}. Successor representation [8] denotes a probability distribution over future states following a policy, implicitly encoding the coupling between the agent’s behaviour and the environment. It can be factored in a low-rank decomposition: forward-backwards representations [2] that encode states, actions, and rewards in the shared latent representation 𝒛∈ℝd{\bm{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Such factorisation allows zero-shot policy inference: given a buffer 𝔻{\mathbb{D}} that is a collection of state-reward pairs (𝒔,r)({\bm{s}},r), the optimal state-action value function QQ can be explicitly computed in a closed form:

Q⁡(𝒔,𝒂)=F​(𝒔,𝒂)⊤​𝒛𝒛=1|𝔻|​∑𝒔,r∈𝔻r​B​(𝒔)\displaystyle\begin{split}Q({\bm{s}},{\bm{a}})=F({\bm{s}},{\bm{a}})^{\top}{\bm{z}}\qquad{\bm{z}}=\frac{1}{|{\mathbb{D}}|}\sum_{{\bm{s}},r\in{\mathbb{D}}}rB({\bm{s}})\end{split} (1)

where FF and BB are forward-backwards representations mapping to the same latent space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. In this article, we use FF and BB parametrised by neural networks, optimised via unsupervised reinforcement learning on human MoCap data and a buffer of 0.5 million state-reward pairs [43]. Such pre-trained representations encode a prior for human-like motion generation and allow the reward to be underspecified: rewarding only for reaching particular state values while other state values follow behaviours encoded in the successor representation.

3.2 ExAct Motion Programs

We design ExAct DSL for generating human-like motions using SPML kinematic model. Each ExAct motion program ϕ\phi represents a procedure for generating motions 𝒔0:T{\bm{s}}_{0:T} from the initial state 𝒔0{\bm{s}}_{0}. To formulate ExAct DSL, we describe its syntax and semantics. For the syntax description, we use a BNF grammar to express the recursive structure of ExAct DSL, with ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle denoting non-terminals in the grammar derivation rules. ExAct motion program BNF grammar is given as follows:

⟨program⟩::=⟨motion⟩|⟨motion⟩;⟨motion⟩⟨motion⟩::=[​t1,t2​]​⟨sensors⟩⟨sensors⟩::=⟨sensor⟩|⟨sensor⟩​⟨sensor⟩⟨sensor⟩::=𝚜𝚙𝚘𝚜​(​x​)\displaystyle\begin{split}\langle\text{program}\rangle&::=\langle\text{motion}\rangle|\langle\text{motion}\rangle;\langle\text{motion}\rangle\\ \langle\text{motion}\rangle&::=\texttt{[}t_{1},t_{2}\texttt{]}\,\langle\text{sensors}\rangle\\ \langle\text{sensors}\rangle&::=\langle\text{sensor}\rangle|\langle\text{sensor}\rangle\langle\text{sensor}\rangle\\ \langle\text{sensor}\rangle&::=\mathtt{s^{pos}}\texttt{(}x\texttt{)}\end{split} (2)

where t1<t2<T∈ℕt_{1}<t_{2}<T\in{\mathbb{N}} are beginning and ending timesteps and x∈[−1,1]x\in[-1,1] is the target position. Each motion program is constructed from one or more motions. Each motion has a timescale defined by its start t1<Tt_{1}<T and end t2<Tt_{2}<T timestep. For example, [0,100]​𝙻𝙰𝚛𝚖.𝚡⁡(0.3)[0,100]\mathtt{LArm.x}(0.3) is a motion program that represents a single motion for 100 timesteps, while [0,300]​𝙻𝙰𝚛𝚖.𝚡⁡(0.3);[300,600]​𝚁𝙰𝚛𝚖.𝚢⁡(0.1)[0,300]\mathtt{LArm.x}(0.3);[300,600]\mathtt{RArm.y}(0.1) represents two motions, each lasting 300 timesteps. Over the timescale of each motion, one or more position sensors 𝚜pos\mathtt{s}^{\mathrm{pos}} like 𝚁𝙰𝚛𝚖.𝚢\mathtt{RArm.y} represent changing the yaw of the right arm joint, and are optimised to reach the target position.

To use ExAct motion programs for human-like motion generation, we compile them to a set of 𝒛t{\bm{z}}_{t} for timesteps for which the ExAct program specified a motion. To this end, we utilise a buffer 𝔻{\mathbb{D}} that encodes partial reward assignments upon reaching the target. To operationalise this, we use the recursive nature of ExAct grammar to define the ExAct semantics:

⟦⟨program⟩⟧=⋃⟨motion⟩∈⟨program⟩⟦⟨motion⟩⟧⟦⟨motion⟩⟧=𝒛t1:t2=1|𝔻|∑s,r∈𝔻⟦⟨sensors⟩⟧B(s)⟦⟨sensors⟩⟧=∏⟨sensor⟩∈⟨sensors⟩⟦⟨sensor⟩⟧⟦⟨sensor⟩⟧=σ⁡((spos−x)2)\displaystyle\begin{split}\llbracket\langle\text{program}\rangle\rrbracket&=\bigcup_{\langle\text{motion}\rangle\in\langle\text{program}\rangle}\llbracket\langle\text{motion}\rangle\rrbracket\\ \llbracket\langle\text{motion}\rangle\rrbracket&={\bm{z}}_{t_{1}:t_{2}}=\frac{1}{|{\mathbb{D}}|}\sum_{s,r\in{\mathbb{D}}}\llbracket\langle\text{sensors}\rangle\rrbracket B(s)\\ \llbracket\langle\text{sensors}\rangle\rrbracket&=\prod_{\langle\text{sensor}\rangle\in\langle\text{sensors}\rangle}\llbracket\langle\text{sensor}\rangle\rrbracket\\ \llbracket\langle\text{sensor}\rangle\rrbracket&=\sigma((s^{\mathrm{pos}}-x)^{2})\end{split} (3)

where 𝒛t1:t2{\bm{z}}_{t_{1}:t_{2}} is applicable for all timesteps in this range, σ\sigma is a sigmoid function, and sposs^{\mathrm{pos}} is the value of joint position 𝚜pos\mathtt{s}^{\mathrm{pos}} for the state ss in 𝔻{\mathbb{D}}. The interpretation of an individual ExAct program ϕ\phi is a collection of the 𝒛{\bm{z}} stored in ⟦ϕ⟧\llbracket\phi\rrbracket. It can be used to compute state-action value using forward-backwards representation in the following closed form:

Qϕ​(𝒔t,𝒂t)=F​(𝒔t,𝒂t)⊤​𝒛tϕ𝒛tϕ={𝒛t1:t2for t∈[t1,t2] and 𝒛t1:t2∈⟦ϕ⟧0otherwise\displaystyle\begin{split}Q_{\phi}({\bm{s}}_{t},{\bm{a}}_{t})&=F({\bm{s}}_{t},{\bm{a}}_{t})^{\top}{\bm{z}}_{t}^{\phi}\\ {\bm{z}}^{\phi}_{t}&=\begin{cases}{\bm{z}}_{t_{1}:t_{2}}&\quad\text{for }t\in[t_{1},t_{2}]\text{ and }{\bm{z}}_{t_{1}:t_{2}}\in\llbracket\phi\rrbracket\\ 0&\quad\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\end{split} (4)

3.3 Parser Training

To parse MoCap data into ExAct motion programs, we train a motion-conditioned code-generation model using an encoder-decoder architecture (see Fig. 2 for an overview). The parser consists of a spatio-temporal graph convolutional network (ST-GCN) encoder ff that embeds MoCap data 𝒔pos0:T{\bm{s}}^{\rm pos}_{0:T} into the latent space of mm motion tokens 𝒄1:m{\bm{c}}_{1:m}. ST-GCN is chosen for its effectiveness for processing MoCap data by exploiting the SPML kinematic model skeleton structure [51]. The generated motion tokens are used as a prefix (similar to LLaVa  [30]) for an autoregressive LLM decoder gg, that incrementally produces the ExAct motion program in the form of a sequence of language tokens yy :

Pr(yi∣y1:i−1,𝒄1:m)=softmax⁡(𝒍i)​s𝒍i=g(𝒄1:m,y1:i−1)𝒄1:m=f(𝒔pos0:T)\displaystyle\begin{split}\Pr(y_{i}\mid y_{1:i-1},{\bm{c}}_{1:m})&=\mathrm{softmax}{({\bm{l}}_{i})s}\\ {\bm{l}}_{i}&=g({\bm{c}}_{1:m},y_{1:i-1})\\ {\bm{c}}_{1:m}&=f({\bm{s}}^{\rm pos}_{0:T})\end{split} (5)

In the encoder ff, all parameters are trainable, while for the decoder, it’s only a small portion using the LoRA fine-tuning [20]. To learn the parser, we use the ExAct grammar (Eq. 2) and forward-backwards representations [43] to produce a dataset of program-motion pairs. Note that we use only the positional component of the state 𝒔pos⊂𝒔{\bm{s}}^{\rm pos}\subset{\bm{s}} for training, since it is equivalent to MoCap data. The parser is trained by minimising the joint loss function:

ℒ=ℒLM+λ​ℒInfoNCE\displaystyle\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\rm LM}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\rm InfoNCE} (6)

that consist of two terms, with relative importance interpolated with λ\lambda:

  • •

    Language modelling (cross-entropy) loss ℒLM\mathcal{L}_{\rm LM} measuring the difference between the surface forms of the predicted and target ExAct motion programs;

  • •

    Contrastive (information noise-contrastive) loss ℒInfoNCE\mathcal{L}_{\rm InfoNCE} [17, 45] that is used to align the motion tokens produced by the encoder to the latent space of the language tokens expected by the decoder.

To ensure the syntactic validity of the produced ExAct motion programs (which is required in model building of executable action models), we utilise the ExAct grammar for grammar-guided generation [44] to enforce the production of strings that are acceptable by the ExAct grammar.

3.4 Model Building

Using the parser, we can parse MoCap data into ExAct motion programs. The unique feature of ExAct motion programs is that they are temporally and functionally compositional: individual ExAct programs can be sequentially merged (concatenating ⟨motion⟩\langle\rm motion\rangle segments) to generate temporally extended motions, and multiple ExAct motion programs can in disjunction influence the reward function in parallel. This allows us to aggregate the set of motion ExAct motion programs Φ\Phi for each action. To composeExAct motion programs into a single executable model, we perform the arithmetic form of logical disjunction of the latent representation of ExAct motion programs as defined in Eq. 4:

QΦ​(𝒔t,𝒂t)=F​(𝒔t,𝒂t)⊤​𝒛tΦ𝒛tΦ=1−∑ϕ∈Φ(1−𝒛tϕ)\displaystyle\begin{split}Q_{\Phi}({\bm{s}}_{t},{\bm{a}}_{t})=F({\bm{s}}_{t},{\bm{a}}_{t})^{\top}{\bm{z}}^{\Phi}_{t}\qquad{\bm{z}}^{\Phi}_{t}=1-\sum_{\phi\in\Phi}(1-{\bm{z}}^{\phi}_{t})\end{split} (7)

Note that for practical purposes, the number of aggregated motion programs per action |Φ||\Phi| is bounded (up to 100 in our experiments) with the selection performed by maximising the diversity of the programs in Φ\Phi, measured by program length, and variety of predicates used in ExAct motion programs.

4 Experiments

The following section discusses an experimental setup for building executable action models (§ 4.1) and using them for downstream tasks of human action segmentation (§ 4.2) and human action anomaly detection (§ 4.3).

4.1 Experimental Setup

In our experiments, we use NVIDIA A100 80GB compute nodes for up to 300 compute hours, including both parser training and experiments using three datasets from two benchmarks. The following benchmarks are considered:

  • •

    HumanAct12 [16] dataset consisting of 90K human poses annotated with 12 action labels (e g. “Walk”, “Run”, “sit down”) gathered from 12 subjects (7 subject data is used for training, 1 for validation, and 6 for testing);

  • •

    EPFL-Smart-Kitchen (ESK) [3] consisting of 29.7 hours of 16 subjects cooking four different recipes with a total of 51 sessions recorded (33 are used for training, 2 for validation, 16 for testing). We consider two datasets that annotate the same sessions but with different granularity of label annotations: ESK Activities that consists of 6 coarse-grained types of action sequences that represent different stages of the recipe execution (e g. “getting ready”, “preparing ingredients”, “cooking”, ”cleaning”) and ESK Verbs consisting of 33 verbs describing fine-grained actions in the kitchen (e g. “add”, “cut”, “stir”, “grab”, “wash”, “switch”).

To learn a parser from MoCap data to ExAct motion programs, we generate a diverse set of 50K ExAct motion programs by varying the number of predicates in a motion program and the generated motion program length and time horizon, up to 1024 timesteps. The programs are further used to generate synthetic MoCap data using forward-backwards representations [43]. We also generate 3K program-motion pairs for validation and use validation data loss for Bayesian optimisation in sweeps for hyperparameter tuning (training for 5 epochs for 10 trials) for parser training (learning rate, weight decay, warm-up steps, gradient accumulation steps, batch size) and the ST-GCN encoder architecture (number of layers, their dimensionality, and the motion token size). For the decoder, we use Qwen2.5-Coder-3B [21] with LoRA [20] with its hyperparameters (rank, alpha, dropout) set as part of hyperparameter sweeps. After several initial training runs, in which we evaluate the scales and importance of two losses, we set λ=0.15\lambda=0.15 before the hyperparameter sweeps to ensure that the parser learns useful encoder representations.

4.2 Human Action Segmentation

Design and Objectives

To evaluate the benefits of executable action models, we consider the task of human action segmentation using human MoCap data, in which, given a sequence of human poses represented in the SPML kinematic model, we assign a label to each timestep (multi-class classification). In these experiments, we explore the utility of executable action models for data augmentation by generating synthetic MoCap data by sampling action sequences from the initial human pose and the executable action model.

Preprocessing, Baselines and Metrics

We use the DLC2Action [23] toolkit, which provides an interface for evaluating a variety of action segmentation models. Following Bonnetto et al. [3] we consider four pose-based action segmentation models: MS-TCN3 [28], EDTCN [26], C2F-TCN [41], and C2F-TRF (C2F-TCN modification that replaces some convolutions with attention). We use DLC2Action to extract features of speed, acceleration, speed direction, joint angles, joint acceleration, intra-coordinate distance, distances to centroids, and centroid positions as is done for ESK pose-based action segmentation baselines (see Appendix of [3] for details). The key difference between our setup and that reported in Bonnetto et al. [3] is that we use the SPML humanoid model rather than the simplified 17-keypoint human pose model. We do that to match ExAct grammar. Note that both HumanAct12 and ESK benchmarks natively record human pose information in the SPML format. We consider segmentation models trained on four types of training datasets:

  • •

    original: original dataset training data;

  • •

    +perturbed: original data as well as data produced with default data augmentations in the DLC2Action toolkit (mirroring, shifting, and adding noise);

  • •

    +synthetic: original data as well as additional 1000 exemplars of data generated using executable action models;

When training the segmentation models, we perform hyperparameter sweeps (10 epochs across 20 trials) and select the best-performing model based on the validation F1 score for each dataset. With the best hyperparameter values, we train each segmentation model for 3 runs (3 random seeds) over 50 epochs and record two performance metrics: segmental F1 score, which measures the model’s effectiveness in determining action boundaries, and action classification and PR-AUC that measure frame-level classification performance.

Results and Discussion

Tables 1, 2 give experimental results. We observe that using executable models for data augmentation (+synthetic) often leads to performance gains without detrimental performance collapse seen with standard data augmentation techniques (+perturbed, e.g., MS-TCN3 ESK Verbs), particularly in fine-grained (small number of action timesteps) datasets. We attribute this difference to the fact that standard data augmentation of +perturbed breaks temporal dependencies in the action sequences. Nevertheless, this proves useful for performance gains on the PR-AUC metric, particularly for ESK Activities. This, nevertheless, can be partially explained by the lower number of action labels in this dataset, with performance degrading for datasets with a greater variety of actions.

When analysing programs generated during dataset parsing, we observe that our parser, although trained on a diverse set of ExAct motion programs with multiple motions, tends to produce simpler motion programs (containing mostly one, sometimes two motion sequences). This, in turn, explains the lack of significant gains from using executable models for the ESK Activities, as data augmentation cannot capture the inherent multifaceted complexity of activities like cooking.

4.3 Human Action Anomaly Detection

Design and Objectives

Executable action models capture the internal mechanics of the action beyond the language description, allowing assessment of the quality and differences between actions. We test this capability on human action anomaly detection, in which, given MoCap data, we estimate how similar/different the MoCap data are across actions for each dataset. As executable models encode the mechanical relationships between actions, such as which actions require the same type of joints, we hypothesise that we can observe such differences compared to scenarios in which we perform human anomaly detection using density estimation that does not explicitly consider the internal structure of the action.

Preprocessing, Baselines and Metrics

We use the training data from each dataset to learn an assessment model for the target action (e.g. “Cut” in ESK Verbs) and use it to measure its compatibility with the query action (e.g.“Add” in ESK Verbs). From each dataset, we use five actions for these experiments. To measure this compatibility using executable models, we use the unordered tree edit distance dedistd_{\mathrm{edist}} [53] between the programs in the executable model ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi and the query action program ψ\psi as an activation for the sigmoid: σ⁡(−dedist​(ϕ,ψ))\sigma(-d_{\mathrm{edist}}(\phi,\psi)). We weight the edit costs, with the highest penalties for using wrong side joints (left instead of right), wrong joints, and wrong joint axes, respectively. In edist\mathrm{edist}, we also ignore differences in temporal scales. We consider three assessment models:

  • •

    normalising-flow (NF): a contemporary density estimator for pose-based human action anomaly detection [19] which uses an ST-GCN encoder to process MoCap data and fit the Gaussian mixture model that allows to estimate the likelihood for each query action instance;

  • •

    mean-sigmoid (mean-σ\sigma): a density estimator based on executable action model that measures the mean response of the sigmoid with the edit distance activation: 1|ϕ|​∑ϕ∈Φσ⁡(−dedist​(ϕ,ψ))\frac{1}{|\phi|}\sum_{\phi\in\Phi}\sigma(-d_{\mathrm{edist}}(\phi,\psi));

  • •

    min-sigmoid (min-σ\sigma): a density estimator based on executable action model that measures the minimum response of the sigmoid with the edit distance activation: arg​minϕ∈Φ⁡σ​(−dedist​(ϕ,ψ))\argmin_{\phi\in\Phi}\sigma(-d_{\mathrm{edist}}(\phi,\psi)).

For evaluation, we use the mean AUC and the AUROC matrix, which records the area under the ROC for the assessment model trained on the target action data and evaluated on different query actions. The AUROC matrix captures in-class and out-of-class differences by enabling us to examine how a model trained on a single action relates to other actions.

Results and Discussion

Fig. 3 shows the AUROC matrices for action comparisons across different datasets as well as mean AUC values. For the ESK Activity dataset, we observe that none of the assessment models captures significant differences between temporary extended actions, as they do not take into account the full complexity of the action (NF limited by the context window, and edit-distance-based models limited by simple program synthesis). For the HumanAct12 dataset, we observe that mean-σ\sigma yields the highest mean AUC. When analysing their AUROC matrices, we see that matrices encode similarities between actions, for example, for “Walk”-“Run”, we observe minimal differences between the programs (which is expected as they joints use are the same for motion generation), while NF ends up discriminating between the two actions, not capturing the clear semantic similarity between actions. This is expected for ExAct programs as they are underspecified and they do not not take into account the spurious cues for action differentiation and just focus on key joints in movement generation, which for “Walk” and “Run” are the same. Finally, for ESK Verbs using executable models we observe a conservative separation profile similar to “Walk” and “Run” in HumanAct12, signalling high similarity between activities, captured by the executable model. Finally, there is a minimal differences in AUROC matrices for mean-σ\sigma and min-σ\sigma method, indicating that low diversity between the target and query action ExAct motion programs.

5 Conclusions

In this paper, we have presented a method for understanding human actions through the lens of executable action models, going beyond a static language description of the activity. By doing so, we demonstrated the complementary benefits of contemporary models for this modelling approach in downstream tasks of human action understanding. As we focus on using MoCap data to learn executable action models, such data is hard to acquire in practice and may not provide sufficient context for tasks; therefore, future work should consider executable models that benefit from multimodal input (e.g., multi-view video data) by leveraging multimodal human motion generation [27].
